zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check aid: [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The supplied page subset was consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription and review notes here are this reviewer’s work, not a reproduction of that dataset. Native scans: Source gallica.bnf.fr / Bibliothèque nationale de France.

runs.text: Veas largas da taboa quando he ſerrada

lines.note: Itame names the broad visible grain of a board. The Portuguese begins a description of how the board is sawn; the uppercase I is visible, and this headword is anticipated by the preceding page’s catchword.

runs.text: direitamente, & de maneira que ficam as ve-

lines.note: The board is sawn so that its grain remains intact. The printed ve- begins veas across the physical line break.

As completes veas. The contrasting term masame introduces another treatment of the board’s grain; the source’s own description is retained rather than rewritten to match modern woodworking definitions.

runs.text: tadas, ou ſerradas por meo de maneira que não

lines.note: Tadas completes cortadas: the grain is cut or sawn through the middle. The following negative clause specifies the resulting appearance.
The grain no longer appears whole and broad. This ends the comparison with masame; the historical verb spelling pareção remains unchanged.
Itame is the transitive verb for causing pain or distress. The principal forms are followed by an example beginning Fi-, which continues into hito wo below.
Hito wo itamuru means causing someone pain or torment. Touo joins the preceding Fi-, and the Portuguese object continues on the next line.
Alguem completes the translation as pain inflicted on someone. This short physical continuation remains separate.
Itamegawa is an untanned hide with its hair removed. The Portuguese historical spelling cortir is retained; the following row describes the hide’s strength and stiffness.

runs.text: mas forte, & dura como de Cauãgos.

lines.note: The hide is nevertheless strong and hard, with Cauãgos supplied as the comparison. The unfamiliar designation and its tilde are preserved as printed; this gloss alone does not settle its precise referent.
Itami is pain or distress. The example itami wo oboyuru begins here, with the visible voboyu- retained at the line end.
Ru completes oboyuru. The Portuguese translates the example as feeling pain or distress.

The verb itamu means suffering pain or distress and also has the further sense introduced by Itẽ. The principal form ǒda is entirely roman; its worn vowel is retained from the aligned draft and is repeated as itǒda in the examples below.

runs.text: Danarſe algũa couſa como peixe freſco, aruore-

lines.note: The additional meaning is going bad or deteriorating, illustrated by fresh fish and a small flowering plant. The printed aruore- continues into the diminutive on the next row.

runs.text: ſinha de craueiro que ſe começa a murchar, &c

lines.note: The diminutive finishes the plant example, which begins to wither. Enlargement and the surviving r and ch support murchar, correcting the OCR muo char without modernizing the surrounding historical forms.
Kono sake ga itōda illustrates sake that has gone bad. The paragraph mark omitted by OCR is visible at the left; the Portuguese translation continues on the next row.

Danado completes the spoiled-sake translation. The explanation names Cami usage and gives sake ga sokoneta; the second o in ſoconeta is worn but its residual curve and the verb support it over OCR ſoceneta. Cami is Japanese embedded in Portuguese.
Sonjita is the alternative wording, with Idem referring to the same spoilage meaning. A figurative extension is then introduced by the printed permet. abbreviation.

runs.text: Dar lhe a alguẽ, ou tocar lhe algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The figurative sense is that something affects or concerns someone. The example introducer is italic and ends with the visible comma; the abbreviations and spaced pronouns are retained.

runs.text: He couſa q̃ me vay, ou to-

lines.note: Itōda koto ja is explained as something that affects or touches the speaker. The Portuguese to- continues into toca on the next row, while the Japanese long-o mark remains a caron.

Ca completes toca. Sashite itamanu koto ja illustrates something that is not especially troubling; the ink patch near the paragraph mark is not an additional letter, and cou has no secure terminal hyphen.

runs.text: ſa que não me dà nada, ou não vai tanto co-

lines.note: Sa completes cousa. The translation says the matter does not affect the speaker, or does not matter so much; co- begins como below.
Mo completes como isso and ends the figurative-use example. The printed ß representation is preserved provisionally.
Itami no mono denotes condolence verses of an epitaph-like kind. Enlargement shows the additional dotted i in epitaphio, correcting the OCR epitapho; the destination of the verses follows below.

runs.text: que ſe mandão em louuor do defunto a caſa do

lines.note: The verses are sent in praise of the deceased to his family’s house. The visible nt sequence gives defunto, not OCR defumo.
The recipient household is that of the father or other relatives. This completes the description of the condolence verses, retaining historical pay.
Itano mono is defined only as certain Japanese articles or pieces. The terse Portuguese does not identify a specific material or object, so the note does not impose one.

runs.text: Certo genero de mariſco como oſtras.

lines.note: Itaragai names a kind of shellfish compared with oysters. The historical Japanese form and the comparison are retained without replacing the headword by a modern species name.

Itari expresses an extreme degree in the example shōchaku no itari nari, conveying great joy. The o has a downward-pointing caron; the worn Portuguese vowel is read as e in Alegrei, supported by the remaining curve and the completed phrase Alegrei me muito.
Me muito completes I rejoiced greatly. Guchi no itari then illustrates the extreme of ignorance; the Portuguese ig- continues into ignorancia.
Norancia completes ignorancia. The upright S. labels written usage and is separated typographically from the italic gloss.
The verb itaru means arriving or entering. The usage note continues ſem/pre across the line break; no hyphen is supplied where the scan does not securely show one.
Pre completes sempre, correcting OCR tre. The example begins zen no michi: the printed consonantal I in Ienno represents the familiar word for virtue and is not changed to J or modern Z.
Zen no michi ni itaru means entering the path of virtue. The gloss prints historical Intrar, which is preserved rather than modernized to Entrar.
Ten ni itaru illustrates entering or reaching heaven. The Portuguese preserves ceo and the source’s two related motion meanings.
Mukashi kara ima ni itari made means from ancient times up to now. Deſdo begins the Portuguese temporal expression and remains the printed historical form.
The translation completes from ancient times until now. A further example begins with virtue or learning, using consonantal Ien and the alternative marker l; gacu- continues as gakumon.
Gakumon ni itatta hito describes someone accomplished in learning, or in virtue with the alternative above. The Portuguese eſ- begins estudo below.
Tudo completes estudo. The next example names Hizen as an alternative destination to Nagasaki; the visible e in Fijen corrects OCR Fijon.

runs.text: Chegar a Fijen, ou a Nã

lines.note: Nagasaki ni itaru completes the destination example. The Portuguese repeats Fijen and divides its abbreviated Nagasaki spelling after Nã; no absent hyphen is invented.
Gaſaqui completes Nãgaſaqui from the preceding line. The scan has a after ſ and no internal word break, correcting OCR gaſo qui.

Itate, itatsuru, itateta concerns shooting an arrow so that it strikes or sticks. The repeated examples and surviving t strokes support Itate and tçuru, not OCR Itare and içuru; the printed aſeta spacing is retained.

Ya wo itatsuru illustrates shooting an arrow. The next example begins teki wo omōsama ni, involving the enemy and forceful shooting; the scan supports Teqiuo and a circumflex in vomôſa-, rather than OCR Toqiuo and a caron.
Mani completes omōsama ni and itateta supplies the past verb. The Portuguese says the shooting made the enemies flee and scatter; Fez, not OCR Foz, is supported by the visible vowel.
The translation specifies arrows or gunfire as the means of scattering the enemies. The historical forms frechadas and eſpingardadas remain unchanged.
Itatte is glossed as profoundly or thoroughly. The example begins with Itat-, not OCR Itai-, and continues onto the last row of this column.

Itatte sorehodo zonjenu says that the speaker does not know to that degree or depth. The row is heavily abraded: surviving f, d, j, and final u strokes, Japanese morphology, and the Portuguese support ſorefodo zonjenu. The gloss reads Não ſei tão profun- and continues as damente at the top of the right column; the reconstructed weak vowels remain a nonblocking caveat.
Damente completes profun- from the bottom of the left column. The translation finishes as not knowing so deeply or at the root of the matter; this is a genuine continuation, not a new entry.
Itasode denotes the sleeve or shoulder components of armor. The headword is flush with the column’s entry margin, so the draft’s continuation indentation is removed.
Itawari gives the principal forms of treating someone with compassion and care. It is a new flush-left headword, not a continuation; fa begins fazer below without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: zer agaſalhado com amor a peßoas fracas, me-

lines.note: Zer completes fazer: the definition includes lovingly welcoming or tending weak people and children. The final me- begins meninos.
Ninos completes meninos. Warambe wo itawari sodatsuru illustrates raising children with affectionate care, preserving the historical warambe form and the divided ſo-.
Datçuru completes sodatsuru. The Portuguese specifies bringing children up with tenderness and love, retaining abbreviated cõ.

runs.text: Couſa de que ſe tem piedade, ou com

lines.note: Itawashii describes something that inspires pity or compassion. The final com continues into compaixão without a visible hyphen.
Paixão completes compaixão. The short indented row belongs to the preceding adjective’s gloss.
Itawashisa is the noun for that pitiable condition. The weak a is part of a single printed word; the OCR space in Ita uaxiſa is removed.
Itawashū is the corresponding adverbial form. The caron over u is preserved, and no Portuguese wording is supplied where none is printed.
Itaoshi denotes felling someone with an arrow or shot. The scan has the contiguous Itauoxi and the abbreviated principal form u; no expected s is silently added to that form.
Pilouro completes the alternative projectile, a ball or bullet. It is part of the shooting definition rather than a separate dictionary item.
Itashi, itasu, itaita is glossed as doing or making. The historical past form aita is retained rather than replaced by modern ashita.
Itaya is a house roofed or covered with boards. The Portuguese directly explains the board-house compound.
Itazugawashii is defined here as being tired and worn out. The historical headword and abbreviated cõ are preserved; the cause follows below.
Trabalho completes being exhausted with work. This ends the gloss before the two short derivative forms.
The indented noun in -ſa belongs to the preceding exhausted or worn-out adjective; the medial long s is visible, and no independent Portuguese gloss is printed.

The indented adverb completes the preceding adjective group. At the far right the scan also prints (ao aluo., omitted from the draft: this completes the arrowhead definition on the following row. It is restored at its actual physical position, not moved into that definition.

runs.text: Ferro da frecha com que apontão

lines.note: This first itazzuqi is the arrowhead used for aiming. The Portuguese clause ends here without a full stop and is completed by the displaced ao aluo. above; the neighboring homograph below is a separate entry.
The second itazzuqi denotes illness or being ill. Restore the visible capital I rather than the draft lowercase i; the gloss and example marker otherwise agree with the scan.
The Japanese formula expresses being ill, matched by Estou doẽte. The nasal abbreviation is visible; the final S. is a roman usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese sentence.
Itazzura is first glossed as idleness. The paragraph introduces another, qualified sense; retain the physical division Aliquan- / do rather than completing the Latin adverb on this row.

runs.text: do per met. Folguedos mundanos, desho-

lines.note: The second sense concerns worldly amusements and dishonesty or unchastity. The scan has a narrow dotted i in Folgueios, not the draft d in Folguedos; preserve this historical i/j spelling. The final desho- continues on the next row.
This completes desho-neſtidade and introduces an example with itazzura. The Japanese is roman after the italic Vt, and the Portuguese explanation of the example starts on the next line.

runs.text: Dar ſe aos goſtos da carne, couſas do mundo,

lines.note: The Portuguese explains the preceding example as giving oneself to bodily pleasures and worldly matters. Keep the printed separate Dar ſe and the historical couſas rather than modernizing either.

runs.text: . Sempre eſta palaura ſe vſa em cõpanhia

lines.note: After &c. the lexicographer says this word is always used in combination. The nasal mark in cõpanhia is visible; retain the draft type boundary around the small c because the worn glyph gives no firm reason to reassign its face.

runs.text: de outras, como ſe vera à baxo.

lines.note: This completes the usage comment: with other words, as will be seen below. The old spelling baxo and the separate à baxo are visible and are not modernized.
Itazzuragoto denotes idle activity. The paragraph and Aliquando introduce an occasional additional sense, whose wording continues below; the headword remains roman.

runs.text: permet. Des honeſtidade, ou paßa tẽpos do mũ-

lines.note: The extended sense is dishonesty or unchastity, or worldly pastimes. Preserve the printed spacing Des honeſtidade and paßa tẽpos, the ligature ß, and the nasal abbreviation with its physical division mũ- / do.
This short indented line completes mũ-do and the preceding gloss. It is a real printed row and remains separate rather than being merged into the longer line above.
The headword denotes an idle or vagrant person. Retain the printed Peſoa and the older initial pri- in pri-guiçoſa, without correcting the dictionary to modern Portuguese spelling.

runs.text: guiçoſa. ¶ Item, Ruim, ou de ruins ma

lines.note: This completes the lazy-person gloss, then adds the sense of a bad person or one of bad habits. The row ends with ma, continued as nhas below; no new hyphen is inferred from faint edge traces.
This short continuation completes ma-nhas, meaning habits or ways. Its indentation and independent physical row are retained.
The adjectival form is glossed as a matter of idleness and easy living. The scan supports ocioſidade, including the tall long s, rather than the draft orioidade; keep boa vida as printed.

This head phrase describes an idle, careless, disobedient person. The last Portuguese word is divided deſobe / diente without a securely visible hyphen; the Japanese mono remains part of the roman head phrase.
This completes deſobe-diente from the preceding row. It remains an indented gloss continuation, with no new headword inferred from its brevity.
The adverb is explicitly labeled Adu. The example begins with roman Itaz, not the draft italic ltaz; retain the printed spelling Ocioſemente and the unhyphenated division into the next row.
The example itazzurani iru means being idle and doing nothing. The split Itaz / zurani is retained, and the upright Japanese type is distinguished from the italic Portuguese explanation.
Itçu is the interrogative when. Both the brief Japanese head and the Portuguese question mark are supported by the scan; this is a separate entry, not a continuation of the adverb example.
The verb means using up arrows or bullets by shooting. Keep the printed three-part form and the division fre- / chas; the head is distinct from the similar-looking beautiful adjective below.
This completes fre-chas and supplies the alternative bullets. Keep pilouros in its printed spelling and this short continuation as a separate physical row.
The adjective means beautiful. The final ij is visible and distinguishes it from the shooting verb above; preserve the older Portuguese fermoſa rather than modern formosa.
This indented -ſa derivative denotes beauty and belongs to the preceding adjective group. The medial long s and the final period are present; no gloss is supplied in the print.
The indented adverbial derivative completes the beautiful-adjective group. Retain the visible long-vowel mark on ǔ and do not supply an unprinted Portuguese gloss.

The headword means showing compassion and affection. A crease and pale ink interrupt the initial It and some following strokes, but the surviving sequence supports Itçucuximi rather than draft Açucux imi. Restore piedade and amor from their visible residual letters and the coherent Portuguese gloss; the damaged initials remain less secure than the rest.

The entry asks when or at what time. A later lexical check prompted enlargement: the worn medial letter lacks the left cross-stroke of t and retains a faint r shoulder, supporting Itçugoro rather than draft Itçugoto. The supplied NINJAL headword agrees, but the correction is made from the scan.

The head means more than ever. The worn ri sequence, partly fused with m, is read as Itçuyorimo rather than draft Itçuyonmo, supported by the visible r and the example continuing as rimo on the next page. Correct nunca from nanca. Retain the period-shaped terminal mark after Itçuyo instead of regularizing it to a hyphen.
